content: United States Adopted Names (USAN) are unique, nonproprietary names assigned to pharmaceuticals marketed in the United States. These names are determined by the USAN Council, which is co-sponsored by the American Medical Association (AMA), the United States Pharmacopeial Convention (USP), and the American Pharmacists Association (APhA). The primary objective of the USAN Council is to create simple, informative, and distinctive nonproprietary names, also referred to as generic names, for drugs. This is achieved by establishing logical nomenclature classifications based on pharmacological and/or chemical relationships. In addition to naming drugs, the USAN Council is also responsible for naming agents used in gene therapy, cell therapy, contact lens polymers, surgical materials, diagnostics, carriers, and excipients. The Council collaborates with the World Health Organization (WHO) International Nonproprietary Name (INN) Expert Committee and other national nomenclature groups to standardize drug nomenclature and establish rules for classifying new substances. The USAN Council was established in June 1961 following the formation of the AMA-USP Nomenclature Committee by the AMA and USP. In 1964, the American Pharmacists Association (APhA) joined as the third sponsoring organization, and the committee was renamed the USAN Council. The term United States Adopted Name became the official designation for any nonproprietary name negotiated and formally adopted by the Council. In 1967, a liaison representative from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) was appointed to the USAN Council. By 1984, the FDA announced it would discontinue adding drug names to its official list and instead use USAN as the established name for labeling and advertising new single-entity drugs marketed in the United States. Currently, the USAN Council consists of five members: one representative from each sponsoring organization, one from the FDA, and one member-at-large. Each sponsoring organization nominates one member annually, and the FDA nominates a liaison member. The member-at-large is selected by the sponsoring organizations from a list of candidates proposed by the AMA, APhA, and USP. All five nominees must be approved annually by the boards of trustees of the three sponsoring organizations. Nonproprietary names, by definition, are not subject to proprietary trademark rights and are entirely in the public domain. This distinguishes them from trademarked names, which are registered for private use. The process of assigning a USAN takes into account practical considerations such as existing trademarks, international harmonization of drug nomenclature, the development of new drug classes, and the potential for changes in the intended uses of substances. Modern USANs reflect both current nomenclature practices and older methods used to name drug entities. Early drug nomenclature was based on chemical structure, but as drugs became more chemically complex and numerous, nonproprietary names based on chemistry became lengthy and difficult to spell, pronounce, or remember. Additionally, chemically derived names often provided little useful information to non-chemist healthcare practitioners. To address these challenges, the USAN system evolved to reflect relationships between new entities and older drugs while avoiding names that might suggest nonexistent relationships. Current nomenclature practices involve the use of standardized syllables, known as stems, which link new chemical entities to existing drug families. Stems may appear as prefixes, suffixes, or infixes in the nonproprietary name and can emphasize specific chemical structures, pharmacologic properties, or a combination of these attributes. The recommended list of USAN stems is regularly updated to accommodate drugs with new chemical and pharmacologic properties. As a general rule, applications for a USAN should be submitted to the USAN Council after the FDA has approved the Investigational New Drug (IND) application and clinical trials have commenced. Many pharmaceutical manufacturers seeking a USAN are multinational companies with subsidiaries worldwide or contractual agreements with drug firms outside the United States. Therefore, it is highly desirable for pharmaceutical companies, nomenclature committees, and the medical community to establish a global name for each new single-entity compound introduced. Assigning a USAN and standardizing names internationally can take anywhere from several months to a few years.
